Bench: K.Lakshman, P.Sree Sudha
 Hon'Ble Sri Justice K. Lakshman
 And
 Hon'Ble Smt. Justice P. Sree Sudha
 Writ Petition No.7680 Of 2023
Common Order:

(Per Hon'ble Sri Justice K. Lakshman) Heard Sri Pasham Trivikram Reddy, learned counsel for the petitioner and Mr. Mujib Kumar Sadasivuni, learned Special Government Pleader representing learned Additional Advocate General appearing on behalf of the respondents.

2. This Writ Petition is filed to issue a writ of Habeas Corpus directing the 3rd respondent to produce the detenu i.e., Janga Venkanna now detained in Central Prison Chanchalguda, Hyderabad and set aside the impugned detention order passed by the 2nd respondent vide SB.ID.No.138/S1/PD-KMM/2022 dated 28.12.2022 and consequential Confirmation order, if any passed by 1st respondent as illegal.
3. Perusal of the record would reveal that five cases were registered against the detenu.
In all these cases, the allegations against the detenu are that he is committing theft by breaking open house and looting.
Therefore, according to respondent No.2, detention order was KL,J & PSS,J passed to prevent the detenu in committing similar offences and on consideration of entire material.

Therefore, the detenu is a habitual offender and to prevent him for committing similar offences,
detention order was passed as per Section 3 of the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activites of Boot-Leggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, Land-Grabbers,
Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders,
Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Document Offenders,
Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders, Sexual Offenders,
Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Respondent No.2 has considered the entire material on record and also nature and manner of offences committed by the detenu.
Therefore, according to learned Special Government Pleader, there is no error in the detention order.
He further submits that the 1st respondent considered the report submitted by the Advisory Board considering the entire material and also nature and manner of offences committed by the detenu.

Therefore, there is no irregularity in confirming the detention order by the 1st respondent vide G.O.Rt.No.270 dated 17.02.2023.
KL,J & PSS,J 4.

Whereas, learned counsel appearing for petitioner would submit that respondents have not filed any application seeking cancellation of bail in subsequent crimes registered against the detenu on the ground that detenu herein has committed similar offences in violation of conditions of bail Janga Rajeshwari, vs The State Of Telangana, on 15 June, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21636116/
1 imposed by the Court below in the 1st crime.

sentences.text: Without taking such steps, respondent No.2 has passed impugned detention order.
5. In Ashok Kumar v. Delhi Administration1, Apex Court observed that preventive detention is devised to afford protection to society.
The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept before he does it and to prevent him from doing.

6. In Sushanta Kumar Banik v. State of Tripura2, the Apex Court held that the preventive detention is a serious invasion of personal liberty and the normal methods open to a person charged with commission of any offence to disprove the charge or to prove his innocence at the trial are not available to the person preventively detained and, therefore, in prevention detention jurisprudence,
whatever little safeguards the Constitution and the enactments .

entities.text: Sushanta Kumar Banik v. State of Tripura2
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1333 KL,J & PSS,J authorizing such detention provide assume utmost importance and must be strictly adhered to.

7. In Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar3, the Apex Court held as under:
"...Does the expression "public order" take in every kind of disorder or only some?

entities.text: Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar3
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The answer to this serves to distinguish "public order" from "law and order" because the latter undoubtedly takes in all of them.
Public order if disturbed, must lead to public disorder.
Every breach of the peace does not lead to public disorder.
When two drunkards quarrel and fight there is disorder but not public disorder.
They can be dealt with under the powers to maintain law and order but cannot be detained on the ground that they were disturbing public order.
Suppose that the two fighters were of rival communities and one of them tried to raise communal passions.
The problem is still one of law and order but it raises the apprehension of public disorder.
Other examples can be imagined.
The contravention of law always affects order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or the public at large.
A mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is thus not necessarily sufficient for action under the Defence of India Act but disturbances which subvert the public order are.
A District Magistrate is entitled to take action under Rule 30(1)(b) to prevent subversion of public order but not in aid of maintenance of law and order under ordinary circumstances.
It will thus appear that just as "public order" in the rulings of this Court (earlier cited) was said to comprehend disorders of less gravity than those .

(1966) 1 SCR 709 KL,J & PSS,J affecting "security of State",
"law and order" also comprehends disorders of less gravity than those affecting public order".
One has to imagine three concentric circles.
Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State.

It is then easy to see that an act may affect law and order but not public order just as an act may affect public order but not security of the State."
8.
Therefore, the detention order can be passed only in rarest of rare cases that too to prevent the detenu from committing similar offences.
It is an extreme step.

2 9.

sentences.text: In VASANTHU SUMALATHA v. STATE OF ANDHRA PRAESH4 it was held that as there is no reference therein to the orders passed by Courts granting conditional bail to the detenu, the detention orders are vitiated by non-consideration of vital and relevant material.

entities.text: VASANTHU SUMALATHA v. STATE OF ANDHRA PRAESH4
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The assertion to the contrary in the counter- affidavits filed before this Court would not justify upholding the,
otherwise, invalid detention orders.
10. Relying on the said principle, a Division Bench of this Court vide order dated 26.07.2021 in W.P.No.12399 of 2021 declared the detention order and confirmation order as illegal.

In another judgment dated 11.06.2020 in W.P.No.4125 of 2020 in Shabana Begum vs. State of Telangana5 it was held that one of the essential requirements for passing an order of detention is that ordinary criminal law is not deterrent upon the detenu and thus, preventive detention law needs to be invoked.

entities.text: Shabana Begum vs. State of Telangana5
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If the detenu can dealt with under ordinary criminal law, there is no need to pass an order of detention under the Act.
To arrive at a conclusion that ordinary criminal law is not capable of dealing with the detenu, there should be a strong case based on sufficient material before the detaining authority.
Mere apprehensions and assumptions would not suffice and by any stretch of imagination, they cannot be the basis for passing the order of detention.
Apart from that, there is also no proper conclusion arrived at by the detaining authority as to how public order is affected.

12. In view of the law laid down in the aforesaid judgment and as discussed supra and coming to the facts of the detenu, though the respondents are claiming that detenu is involved in five cases and they have not taken steps either opposing bail application in the aforesaid crimes or filed applications seeking to cancel the bail granted to the detenu on the ground that he has committed similar offences.

In all the aforesaid five crimes, the allegations against the detenu are KL,J & PSS,J committing theft, looting, break upon the lock etc. and the offences alleged are punishable under Sections 457, 380 of IPC.
In the impugned order, there is no consideration of the aspect that offences committed by the detenu disturbed the public order.
Without taking such steps, respondent No.2 cannot invoke the procedure laid down under the Telangana Act of 1986.
13. The detenu was released on 25.11.2022 on bail and the detention order was passed on 28.12.2022 i.e., after one month three days.
There is no consideration of the said aspect in the detention order and in the confirmation order.
Therefore, both the orders are liable to be set aside and accordingly it is set aside.
This Writ Petition is allowed, detention order dated 28.12.2022 of respondent No.2 confirmed by respondent No.1 vide G.O.Rt.No.270 dated 17.02.2023 was set aside.

Respondents are directed to set the detenu i.e., Janga Venkanna, father Veeraiah, age 31 years,
Occupation painter, Residence Regulachelaka Village, Raghunathapalem Mandal, Khammam District, Telangana State, free forthwith if he is no longer required in any other criminal case.
In the circumstances of the case, there shall be no order as to costs.
KL,J & PSS,J
As a sequel, the miscellaneous petitions, if any, pending in the writ petitions shall stand closed.
